site-2190.title: Acanceh
site-2190.description:
INAH’s guide describes an ancient settlement extending across roughly three square kilometres beneath and around the modern town. Its main pyramid was originally decorated with eight large stucco masks beside four stairways. Early photographs and surviving fragments helped researchers document decoration that had already disappeared from part of the building by the 1930s. The masks made sacred imagery visible in a public ceremonial setting.

The Palace of the Stuccoes stands on a substantial platform. Its small rooms and earlier construction suggest ritual use, while later buildings on the platform may have served administrative purposes. The painted frieze combines stylized mammals, birds and other supernatural figures within stepped frames; ochre, green and red were prominent colours. The guide interprets this imagery in relation to the celestial realm and the ruling lineage, while treating the precise identities of the figures as uncertain.

site-4955.title: Aké
site-4955.description:
INAH’s guide distinguishes several building phases within the enormous Building of the Pilasters. Its upper platform carried 35 stone supports, assembled from large blocks and weathered into column-like forms. Later occupants built small rooms over part of this space, reusing or removing some supports. These changes show how monumental places acquired different functions over time.

The guide also describes Aké’s settlement beyond the central plaza: modest room foundations contrast with residences on raised stone platforms. An approximately 32-kilometre causeway connected Aké with Izamal, while other causeways linked groups within the city. Part of the long road was later covered by a surrounding wall. That sequence raises questions about changing regional relationships, although the exact political events behind it remain interpretations rather than established facts.

sources.label: INAH · Aké archaeological guide (1991)
sources.author: Rubén Maldonado Cárdenas
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-5004.title: Hochob
site-5004.description:
The hilltop was deliberately levelled to make room for connected plazas, houses and ceremonial buildings. INAH’s guide places Hochob’s strongest architectural flowering around AD 850–1000. Its small size does not diminish the complexity of its stone façades. Structure II’s entrance turns the entire doorway into an enormous sacred mouth, with teeth, ear ornaments and stacked profile masks integrated into the masonry.

Early descriptions record a decorated roof-comb above this building, most of which has disappeared. Another group combines Chenes-style imagery with towers and simulated stairways associated with Río Bec architecture. Openings beside the buildings lead to underground rainwater cisterns. These reservoirs help explain how a community sustained itself on a raised limestone site without a permanent surface water supply.

sources.label: INAH · Hochob archaeological guide (2002)
sources.author: Renée Lorelei Zapata Peraza
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-1226.title: Hormiguero
site-1226.description:
Hormiguero lies near the meeting of the Río Bec and Petén architectural regions. Structure II preserves an especially elaborate south façade: a central monster-mouth entrance is flanked by tower forms and additional ornamented doorways. The building contained eight rooms in two parallel ranges. Its rear façade was comparatively plain, with a portico whose columns probably supported a perishable roof.

INAH’s guide describes an earlier building beneath this structure, demonstrating that the celebrated façade belongs to a sequence of rebuilding. In the Central Group, Structure V rises above a vaulted passage and repeats some of the larger building’s tower and mask motifs on a smaller scale. The contrast between its surviving west side and damaged east side makes the difference between preserved fabric and reconstruction particularly important.

sources.label: INAH · Hormiguero archaeological guide (1999)
sources.author: Ángeles Cantero Aguilar
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-5187.title: Ichkabal
site-5187.description:
The 2025 INAH guide presents Ichkabal as a landscape of monumental platforms, plazas, causeways and engineered water storage. Structures 4 and 5 are triadic acropolises, each arranging three temples on a raised platform. At Structure 5, superimposed stairways reveal successive construction stages, while surviving stucco masks retain evidence of the buildings’ former decoration. Much of the immense Structure 1 remains beneath vegetation.

Beside the main plaza, an artificial reservoir known as the Crocodile Pool provided stored water and now supports wetland wildlife. Offerings associated with Structure 7 included Pacific shells and jade from Guatemala, connecting this inland settlement with wider exchange networks. The guide also describes an E-Group arrangement used to mark solar events. Such evidence links architecture with ritual, seasonal observation and the practical demands of urban life.

sources.label: INAH · Ichkabal archaeological guide (2025)
sources.author: INAH
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-1193.title: Kohunlich
site-1193.description:
INAH’s guide places the civic and residential core on the higher western plain, with lower eastern ground supporting food production and water storage. The Yaxná group preserves some of the earliest monumental construction and high-status burials. Later growth produced varied neighbourhoods rather than a single compact temple precinct.

The Las Vías group yielded unfinished stone tools and flint-working debris, providing evidence of craft activity. The Pixa’an and Twenty-Seven Steps groups preserve substantial residential compounds, while the Merwin Plaza contains buildings with several forms of columns and porticoes. Later platforms and offerings among abandoned buildings indicate that parts of the settlement remained in use after its major construction projects had ceased. The celebrated stucco masks are interpreted in the guide as royal or ancestral figures bearing solar attributes, connecting rulership with sacred imagery.

sources.label: INAH · Kohunlich archaeological guide (2019)
sources.author: INAH
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-1228.title: Becán
site-1228.description:
Becán’s monumental core was enclosed by a ditch and parapet, with seven crossings providing access. INAH’s guide notes that the ditch may initially have drained excess rainwater before serving defensive purposes. Most inhabitants lived outside this enclosure, so the prominent ruins represent a restricted centre within a wider settlement.

Structure VIII combines a long palace, eight rooms and tall lateral towers; an interior passage connects additional vaulted chambers. Structure X forms part of a complex of courtyards and many rooms, including a central palace with benches, niches and fittings for curtains. Successive construction concealed parts of this earlier arrangement beneath stepped platforms. At Structure IX, excavations identified multiple phases and recovered a group of ceramic vessels whose imagery and inscriptions contribute to the site’s history.

sources.label: INAH · Becán archaeological guide (2015)
sources.author: Antonio Benavides Castillo
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-1946.title: Izapa
site-1946.description:
The INAH guide emphasizes Izapa’s place in the Mixe-Zoque cultural region and its connections with artistic traditions that later flourished across the Maya world. Groups of earthen mounds enclose plazas where stelae and altars were carefully positioned. Later buildings in Group F used river stones from the nearby Izapa River as facing material.

The carved monuments combine people, animals and supernatural beings in complex scenes. Some arrange imagery into celestial, earthly and underworld zones. The guide interprets Stela 5’s great tree as an axis linking those realms, while other carvings depict ritual, rulership and mythological action. These are interpretations of a distinctive sculptural tradition, not a fully deciphered written account. The setting beneath the volcanic highlands forms an important part of the site’s wider landscape.

sources.label: INAH · Izapa archaeological guide (2018)
sources.author: Víctor Manuel Ortiz Villarreal , Traductor (trl): Violeta Hinojosa Navarro , Productor (pro): Centro Cultural de los Altos de Chiapas
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-4935.title: Kabah
site-4935.description:
Kabah’s main architectural groups occupy raised parts of the terrain, with large platforms organizing plazas and controlling access between public and more restricted spaces. INAH’s guide links the Eastern Group with both royal residence and civic or religious activity during the city’s principal flowering.

The Codz Poop was altered over time: a later wing added rooms and imagery that included human figures and latticework associated with political authority. This has supported an interpretation of part of the building as a council house. In the plaza, a comparatively small altar bears inscriptions on four sides. Its damage complicates reading the original text, but surviving signs provide evidence for connections with Uxmal. The guide also records a long causeway between the two cities, placing Kabah within a broader Puuc network.

sources.label: INAH · Kabah archaeological guide (2018)
sources.author: José Guadalupe Huchim Herrera
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-4769.title: Izamal
site-4769.description:
Izamal’s ancient settlement extended beyond the modern town. INAH’s guide describes a major plaza framed by monumental religious buildings and a causeway network reaching surrounding communities. Residential remains along the road to Aké show that movement between centres also passed through inhabited landscapes.

The Itzamatul platform preserves several construction stages, with an earlier stepped building eventually enclosed inside a much larger base. At Kabul, nineteenth-century drawings and investigations recorded stucco decoration that no longer survives. Other groups, including Habuc and Chaltunha, preserve different parts of the city’s architectural history. The Franciscan monastery was erected over another major pre-Hispanic platform, transforming the southern edge of the ancient plaza. Izamal therefore offers a layered urban landscape in which later construction both damaged and incorporated earlier monuments.

sources.label: INAH · Izamal archaeological guide (2001)
sources.author: Luis Alfonso Millet Cámara
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-4944.title: La Venta
site-4944.description:
La Venta is an Olmec centre included in the source atlas’s wider regional inventory. Its main occupation lasted approximately 1200–400 BC. Civic and ceremonial buildings occupied a natural rise above flood-prone ground, while surrounding households combined farming with the use of forest and aquatic resources. Monumental stone had to be brought from beyond the local area.

INAH’s guide describes Complex A’s carefully arranged courtyards, basalt columns, burials and extraordinary buried offerings. Some deposits contained mosaics assembled from hundreds of greenstone blocks; Offering 4 arranged sixteen small figures in a semicircle. Their precise meanings remain debated. Stone-lined channels at the Stirling Acropolis add evidence for water management. Many original sculptures were moved to museums during twentieth-century development, so some monuments displayed at the archaeological site are replicas rather than the excavated originals.

sources.label: INAH · La Venta archaeological guide (2000)
sources.author: Rebecca Bell González Lauck
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-3555.title: Labná
site-3555.description:
Labná’s central buildings occupy a valley surrounded by residential hills. INAH’s guide distinguishes earlier construction around the southern ceremonial area from later enlargement of the Palace complex. The Palace grew through several stages, with earlier rooms and patios incorporated into a much larger platform and rows of vaulted chambers. Unfinished rooms in its northeastern sector preserve evidence that the final project was never completed.

A relief associated with Room 19 contains a date corresponding to AD 862; the guide suggests it may commemorate the dedication of a throne room. A causeway linked the Palace with the sacred precinct near the Mirador and Arch. The buildings also show changes within Puuc architecture, from relatively plain walls and stucco roof decoration to elaborate stone mosaics. Numerous underground cisterns supplied stored rainwater within the settlement.

sources.label: INAH · Labná archaeological guide (2015)
sources.author: José Guadalupe Huchim Herrera
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-4931.title: Loltún
site-4931.description:
Loltún preserves evidence of uses that extend well beyond a single Maya building period. Its chambers sheltered early inhabitants of the peninsula and later became settings for ritual activity. Carved water-catching basins, altered rock surfaces and an altar show how people adapted the natural cave rather than constructing a conventional temple precinct.

At the Nahkab entrance, a relief depicts a richly dressed standing figure with a spear and elaborate headdress. Elsewhere, painted hands, animals, human figures and stepped designs survive on the rock. These traces belong to different episodes of use; they should not be read as one contemporary decorative program. The INAH guide also describes barriers associated with the nineteenth-century Caste War, a reminder that the cave's history continued long after the ancient cities changed.

sources.label: INAH · Loltún archaeological guide (2018)
sources.author: José Guadalupe Huchim Herrera , Traductor (trl): Victoria Padilla Bernal , Productor (pro): Centro Cultural de los Altos de Chiapas
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-1232.title: Mayapán
site-1232.description:
Mayapán's surviving paintings add an intimate counterpoint to its walls and monumental pyramid. The INAH guide describes painted niches, serpent imagery and aquatic scenes that once gave several buildings vividly colored surfaces. In the Temple of the Painted Niches, miniature temple fronts appear above serpent heads; the Fisherman's Temple includes a scene involving a person, fish and an alligator.

Another painted ensemble beside the Castillo shows richly dressed figures holding a circular solar emblem against blue. These details connect architecture with imagery also encountered in painted manuscripts and wider Mesoamerican traditions. The guide cautions against treating the famous alliance of Mayapán, Uxmal and Chichén Itzá as a straightforward contemporary federation: archaeological evidence places their principal periods of prominence at different times. The city's history requires both documentary traditions and excavation evidence.

sources.label: INAH · Mayapán archaeological guide (2019)
sources.author: Carlos Alberto Peraza Lope
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-1224.title: Calakmul
site-1224.description:
Calakmul's buildings preserve successive construction projects inside later monuments. The INAH guide describes earlier architecture enclosed within Structure II, including monumental masks and a broad decorated frieze. Rebuilding incorporated these earlier works into a larger architectural mass, so the visible exterior represents only part of the monument's history.

The Chik Naab complex offers a different kind of evidence: paintings with a broad color palette and carefully rendered clothing survive on a buried building. Elite residences and richly furnished burials in the Great Acropolis further distinguish palace life from the public plazas. The guide emphasizes that the city's development continued after its defeat by Tikal in 695, while later offerings and incense burners indicate visits after royal power had declined. Political defeat, urban change and the end of ritual activity were separate processes.

sources.label: INAH · Calakmul archaeological guide (2015)
sources.author: Ramón Carrasco Vargas
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-2116.title: Muyil
site-2116.description:
Muyil comprises several architectural groups rather than a single compact monument. The INAH guide distinguishes its principal precinct, a cenote group and western remains, with local causeways connecting parts of the settlement. The buildings visible on a visit represent only a portion of the ancient community, whose location also connected it with lagoon resources and regional movement.

The Castillo combines a tall temple platform with an unusual solid circular element above the sanctuary; the guide leaves that feature's function unresolved. Traces of red and Maya blue paint recall the buildings' former appearance. Temple 8 preserves successive stairways and an inner sanctuary enclosed by later construction, with painted surfaces surviving within. Differences between earlier architecture and later East Coast forms make Muyil especially useful for following changing building traditions through time, without assuming that every visible structure belongs to the same phase.

sources.label: INAH · Muyil archaeological guide (1991)
sources.author: Elia del Carmen Trejo Alvarado
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-2816.title: Lagartero
site-2816.description:
Lagartero's inhabitants adapted an island and wetland landscape. The main civic and ceremonial precinct occupies Limonal Island, while smaller remains around the marsh reflect a wider settlement. Fishing and hunting supplemented maize and cotton farming; imported obsidian and other goods connected the community with distant regions.

The INAH guide describes terraced buildings arranged around plazas and smaller courtyards, together with a ballcourt. On two pyramids, recessed forms resemble an inverted T, a motif interpreted by some researchers as a reference to wind. The Guajil Pyramid has a broad stairway rising through its stepped platform to the remains of a temple. Excavated figurines preserve unusually specific details of clothing and headdresses, while broken pottery and animal remains provide evidence for ceremonial deposits. These finds bring household life, exchange and ritual into the history of the same marshland community.

sources.label: INAH · Lagartero archaeological guide (2018)
sources.author: Gabriel Lalo Jacinto , Traductor (trl): Violeta Hinojosa Navarro , Productor (pro): Centro Cultural de los Altos de Chiapas
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-3928.title: Mitla
site-3928.description:
Mitla is a Zapotec city in Oaxaca, retained here as part of the original atlas's broader Mesoamerican inventory. Its principal later palaces developed after Monte Albán's decline. Five monumental groups preserve different layouts: some arrange platforms around open plazas, while others organize residential and administrative rooms around enclosed courtyards.

The Hall of the Columns contains large monolithic supports that once carried its roof. Nearby rooms display mosaics assembled from finely cut stones into intricate geometric panels; the individual pieces of this decorative work fit together without mortar. Cross-shaped tombs beneath the southern complex continue the architectural decoration below ground. The Church Group also preserves traces of manuscript-like mural painting and the later insertion of the Church of Saint Paul. Together, the buildings record a specifically Zapotec architectural tradition and the transformation of an inhabited place through the colonial period.

sources.label: INAH · Mitla archaeological guide (2017)
sources.author: Agustín Enrique Andrade Cuautle
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-4937.title: Sayil
site-4937.description:
Sayil's layout joins monumental architecture with productive land. The INAH guide describes major stone building groups linked along a roughly north–south axis, with houses and cultivated plots between them. Fertile valley soils helped shape settlement choices despite the scarcity of accessible water; nearby Chaak Cave was one important water source.

The North Palace grew through several construction phases, but repeating columns, entrances and decorative forms gave the finished facade a coherent rhythm. Its functions extended beyond ceremony: a kitchen identified in the northwest part supports residential use alongside political and administrative activity. Sculpted monuments suggest rulers, while other archaeological evidence points to power shared among important lineages. This combination of palace design, dispersed housing and cultivation makes the city more complex than a single royal residence surrounded by empty jungle.

sources.label: INAH · Sayil archaeological guide (2018)
sources.author: José Guadalupe Huchim Herrera
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-2810.title: Tenam Puente
site-2810.description:
Tenam Puente's Acropolis was created by repeatedly leveling and terracing a hill. Its different elevations directed movement between plazas and more restricted spaces. The INAH guide distinguishes this highland building tradition from lowland Maya architecture: corbelled stone vaults were not used here, and several buildings have substantial sloping retaining walls.

Three ballcourts show the importance of ritual gatherings. The largest occupies an open plaza below the Acropolis, where a considerable audience could assemble. Burials placed within Building 7 included objects from distant regions, while a tomb in Building 21 contained jadeite, marine shells and a carved bone serpent. These finds connect the hilltop community with wider exchange networks. Modeled stucco on Building 29 included Venus and death-related imagery, adding another layer to the way architecture framed ritual experience.

sources.label: INAH · Tenam Puente archaeological guide (2016)
sources.author: Gabriel Lalo Jacinto , Productor (pro): Centro Cultural de los Altos de Chiapas
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-5153.title: Toniná
site-5153.description:
Toniná's Acropolis is a densely organized architectural landscape. Seven rising platforms carry courts, passages, palaces and temples, with successive stairways controlling access as people moved upward. In his INAH guide, archaeologist Juan Yadeun Angulo interprets this arrangement as a ceremonial ordering of space tied to celestial cycles; that symbolic reading is an interpretation of the architecture rather than a surviving written plan.

The palace areas preserve suites of rooms around interior courts, alongside more austere ranges elsewhere in the complex. Sculpture and modeled stucco made political and ritual messages part of these surroundings, including representations of captives and cosmic imagery. The ballcourt occupied a lower space beside the watercourse. Later reuse altered buildings and monuments after the city's principal royal period, so damaged sculptures and architectural modifications also belong to Toniná's long history.

sources.label: INAH · Toniná archaeological guide (2012)
sources.author: Juan Yadeun Angulo
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-4981.title: Tres Zapotes
site-4981.description:
Tres Zapotes belongs to the Olmec and Epi-Olmec world of Veracruz, rather than being a Maya city. The original atlas includes it within its wider regional coverage. Its major mound groups occupy an alluvial plain and natural terraces near a stream, with separate plazas distributed across the settlement.

The INAH guide emphasizes the site's long sequence through the transition from Olmec traditions into later regional developments. Stela C preserves an early Long Count calendar inscription, while colossal heads and other carved monuments document public imagery and authority. Investigations of pottery established a lengthy regional chronology. Volcanic deposits also affected the settlement landscape, and researchers have considered whether eruptions helped shift occupation toward higher terraces. The earth mounds, sculpture and environmental evidence therefore tell complementary parts of the story, rather than reducing the site to its famous heads.

sources.label: INAH · Tres Zapotes archaeological guide (2000)
sources.author: María del Pilar Caro Sánchez
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-5008.title: Oxkintok
site-5008.description:
Oxkintok's architecture records a long sequence of experimentation. The INAH guide follows changes from early regional forms toward the better-known Puuc tradition, including improvements in stone cutting and vault construction. Its principal Ah Dzib, Ah May and Ah Canul groups concentrate buildings on large platforms connected by causeways, while smaller groups extend around them.

The Satunsat is especially distinctive: a multilevel building with a maze-like arrangement of vaulted passages and chambers, partly adapted to the underlying rock. Small wall openings admitted light or air; proposed astronomical and cosmological functions remain interpretations. Later offerings and alterations in the Ah Canul Group show that some places continued to matter after the city's political importance diminished. Oxkintok thus preserves both changing architectural techniques and the reuse of established sacred settings.

sources.label: INAH · Oxkintok archaeological guide (2015)
sources.author: Luis Raúl Pantoja Díaz , Diseñador (dsr): Manuel Cózar
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico

site-2737.title: Pomoná
site-2737.description:
Pomoná occupied a strategic setting between the coastal plain and routes along the Usumacinta. The INAH guide presents control of movement through this landscape as a possible reason for rivalry involving Palenque and Piedras Negras. Captives associated with Pomoná appear on Piedras Negras Stela 12, placing the city within documented regional conflict.

The settlement was dispersed among six major architectural groups. Builders transported limestone from the nearby foothills to create platforms and sculpted monuments. In Group I, a large open plaza is framed by higher structures on the north and west and lower platforms on the east. Building 3 is notable for stairway slabs bearing solar imagery. Building 1 retains a fragmentary circular altar in front of its main stairway. These surviving details connect the city's political history with the organization of its public spaces.

sources.label: INAH · Pomoná archaeological guide (2017)
sources.author: Ito J. Kato Vidal
sources.credit: National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), National Coordination of Dissemination; © Ministry of Culture, INAH, Mexico
